title: Handcuffs and Backup Centers
brief: Which backups would step into a big role if the starter ahead of them misses time, and which of them have value on their own? It must explain that in our daily league with 2 bench spots most handcuffs are waiver pickups, not draft stashes.
summary: In our 12-team daily league, only a few backups have value on their own: guards and forwards who give real categories while the starter plays. Draft those late and cheap. Most pure handcuffs, especially backup centers, belong on waivers. We have only 2 bench spots and daily FAB, so the right move is to add a backup the day his starter goes down, not to stash him in the auction.

paragraphs.text: A basketball handcuff is not a football handcuff. He must give you something while the starter is healthy, and then have big upside if the starter gets hurt. A backup who gives nothing until an injury is not a handcuff for us. He is a waiver name.

The best case is a clear one-for-one backup. If the starter goes down, he would start and play 30 or more minutes. Check this before you value any backup. Being listed as the backup point guard is not enough. When a team has several ball handlers, wings can take the minutes instead.

Count how many players sit ahead of him in the rotation. With one player in front, one injury gives him minutes. If he needs several teammates hurt before he matters, he is not a draft pick, however good his upside looks.

Some role players also gain when a teammate misses time, even if they are not the direct backup. Their usage goes up. The notes give McDaniels as an example. These players already have a role, so their upside comes on top of real value.

sections.heading: Why most handcuffs are waiver pickups here

paragraphs.text: Our roster has only 2 bench spots and daily lineups. A stash that gives you nothing ties up one of your two flexible spots for weeks. That spot is worth more for streaming games and for a waiver add when news breaks. Each week allows up to 6 acquisitions, and FAB runs every day, so you can react to an injury within a day.

Several notes warn against paying for injury upside. A late pick should have a realistic path to a role. Waiting for someone else to get hurt is not a plan, and players who only pay off after an injury make poor late picks. With 144 players drafted, the backups ranked outside the pool will still be on waivers when the injury comes.

What to do: in the auction, spend real money only on backups who are worth rostering while the starter is healthy. Pay 1 USD for pure handcuffs, and only in the last rounds. For everyone else, keep a watch list of backup and starter pairs. When a starter is ruled out for more than a few games, put in a FAB bid for his backup. If you own the injured starter, move him to one of your 4 IL spots first so you keep both players.

The experts split on late stashes. One side says backups who are one injury from starting are fine late flyers, and that a late pick can insure a star if you take the teammate who would start in his place. The other side says upside that needs someone else's injury should not be relied on, and that such players are poor late picks. For our league, both views point to the same rule. Use one of your last 1 USD picks on a backup only if he is a clear one-for-one starter in waiting and gives some value now. Leave the others on waivers.

The experts also disagree on backup centers. One note says a backup center is not worth rostering until the starter in front of him is out. Another says a backup big with strong per-minute production is worth drafting, because he becomes valuable the moment the starter misses time. The middle ground: draft a backup big only if his per-minute numbers are strong. Do not draft one just to wait for a trade. That is usually a waste, especially if he is not a strong per-minute producer.

Backup centers are still very useful during the season. When they start in place of a resting starter, they can be elite streamers for FG%, rebounds and blocks. They also pick up extra minutes when the starter is in foul trouble, hurt or not scoring. With daily lineups, use one of your bench spots to stream these spot starts.

Watch the backup center battles behind injury-prone starters. Whoever wins those starts will have fantasy value. Prefer a backup who can play back-to-backs and whose minutes can be pushed. He gives a steadier line than a big who has his own injury limits.

For each backup on your watch list, check four things in the first two weeks. Who starts on opening night. His minutes compared with the 30-minute bar for a true handcuff. Whether other players are also competing for the role. The health and rest pattern of the starter ahead of him. When the answer to the last one changes, bid that day. Do not wait for the weekly reset.

Before a handcuff add, also check the schedule for weeks 19 to 21. A backup on a team with few playoff games, or one who sits back-to-backs, is worth less to hold into March. Use him as a short-term fill-in and drop him when the starter returns.
